byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: The census of 1931 counted 350 million people, of whom fewer than one in ten could read and write a postcard.

items.title: Population
items.summary: The census of 1931 counted 350.5 million people, up from 316.1 million in 1921.

items.title: Who could write a postcard
items.summary: By 1931, 9.5 percent of the population could read and write a postcard.
items.metric: Share who could read and write a postcard

items.title: Languages counted
items.summary: The 1931 census noted 225 languages; George Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India had recorded 179 languages and 544 dialects.

byTheNumbers.scarcityNote: Urban share, life expectancy and household figures are not in the sources we could open for 1930-31.

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.standfirst: Salt, a necessity at every meal, was the year's political question; see the spotlight.

items.title: Selling tea to Indians
items.summary: The Indian tea industry ran campaigns in the 1930s, with free samples and tea stalls at stations, to turn tea into a daily drink at home.

items.title: Irani cafés
items.summary: Irani cafés in Bombay and Pune served tea, bun maska and keema pav at low prices and became meeting places.

items.title: Millets and pulses
items.summary: Most villagers ate millet, rice or wheat with pulses, vegetables and chillies, and meat or milk were occasional.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: The boycott of foreign cloth and khadi are covered in the spotlight.

items.title: The Gandhi cap
items.summary: The white khadi cap, worn by Congress supporters, became a political statement, and wearers were sometimes arrested for it.

items.title: The Nivi drape spreads
items.summary: The Nivi style of draping, with the pleats tucked at the waist and the end over the shoulder, spread across many regions.

items.title: Western clothes in town
items.summary: Lawyers, clerks and students in cities wore shirts, trousers or coats, often with a cap or turban.

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: After 1929 world prices of crops such as jute, cotton and wheat fell, and many farmers had trouble paying rent and debts.

items.title: The Depression reaches the farm
items.summary: After 1929 world prices of crops such as jute, cotton and wheat fell, and many farmers had trouble paying rent and debts.

items.title: Mill strikes in Bombay
items.summary: Textile workers in Bombay struck in 1928 and 1929 over wages and work rules, and the government passed the Trade Disputes Act in 1929.

items.title: Steel at Jamshedpur
items.summary: Tata Steel's plant at Jamshedpur, begun in 1907, employed thousands and ran a company town with houses and schools.

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: Most children who started school left before they could read well.

items.title: Starting school and leaving it
items.summary: Of every 100 children who began Class I in 1922-23, only 18 were still reading in Class IV in 1925-26, the figure behind the Hartog Committee's report on wastage in 1929.
items.metric: Of 100 who began Class I (1922-23), number in Class IV (1925-26)

schoolAndChildhood.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1930 school enrolment or fees.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: The Frontier Mail began running between Bombay and Peshawar in 1928 and was one of the best-known trains.

items.title: Frontier Mail
items.summary: The Frontier Mail began running between Bombay and Peshawar in 1928 and was one of the best-known trains.

items.title: The first airmail service
items.summary: In October 1932 J.R.D. Tata flew mail from Karachi to Bombay, the start of Tata Airlines.

items.title: Hand-pulled rickshaws
items.summary: In Calcutta men pulled passengers in hand rickshaws, and trams ran on the main roads.

items.title: Bullock carts and tongas
items.summary: Away from rail lines, people went by bullock cart, horse tonga or on foot.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: The government took over broadcasting in 1930 as the Indian State Broadcasting Service, which became All India Radio in 1936.

items.title: Radio begins
items.summary: The government took over broadcasting in 1930 as the Indian State Broadcasting Service, which became All India Radio in 1936.

items.title: Letters by air
items.summary: Airmail had started in 1911 with a demonstration flight at Allahabad, and regular air services shortened letter times in the 1930s.

items.title: Papers and pamphlets
items.summary: Nationalist newspapers and pamphlets spread news of the Salt March, though some were banned or fined.

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine
healthAndMedicine.standfirst: Cholera, plague, smallpox and malaria were common, and vaccination and quinine were the main defences.

items.title: Cholera, plague and malaria
items.summary: Cholera, plague, smallpox and malaria were common, and vaccination and quinine were the main defences.

items.title: All-India Institute of Hygiene
items.summary: The All-India Institute of Hygiene and Public Health opened in Calcutta in 1932.

sources.label: Wikipedia: All India Institute of Hygiene and Public Health

items.title: Medical Council Act
items.summary: The Indian Medical Council Act of 1933 set up a body to register doctors.

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.standfirst: The silent cinema was an outing for four annas, and the first talkies were a few months away.

items.title: A cinema ticket
items.summary: A regular cinema ticket cost four annas; at the opening of the first Indian talkie, Alam Ara, in Bombay in March 1931, such tickets reportedly changed hands at Rs 5.

sources.label: Outlook India: The Ghost Who Talked (Alam Ara)
Live History India: Alam Ara, Indian cinema finds its voice

items.originalUnits: 4 annas (a quarter of a rupee; 16 annas = 1 rupee)

items.title: Halls ready for sound
items.summary: By the end of 1930 about 30 cinema halls in India could screen talkies, ahead of Alam Ara in March 1931.

sources.label: Outlook India: The Ghost Who Talked (Alam Ara)

leisureAndFun.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced material on festivals or sport as ordinary people took part in 1930.

spotlight.title: Salt and khadi in everyday life
spotlight.standfirst: Salt was something every household needed, and a government monopoly on it turned a pinch from the kitchen into the year's act of civil disobedience, with women at the front.

items.title: A monopoly on salt
items.summary: Under the Salt Act of 1882 the government held a monopoly on salt, so people had to buy it from colonial depots even though coastal families could make it by boiling seawater.

items.title: The poor's tax
items.summary: Historians note that the salt tax weighed most heavily on India's poor, though every household needed salt; Gandhi called salt 'next to air and water, perhaps the greatest necessity of life'.

items.title: Women at the picket line
items.summary: Gandhi suggested women were best suited to picketing liquor shops and sellers of foreign cloth and to spinning khadi yarn, a programme that led to an unprecedented number of women's arrests.

sources.label: South Asia (Taylor & Francis), 2023: article on women and civil disobedience
Scroll.in: How Mumbai suburban women contributed to the freedom struggle

items.title: Bombay's women
items.summary: Through 1930-31 women in Bombay's suburbs led processions, picketed foreign-cloth shops, hoisted Congress flags and broke the salt laws, and an unprecedented number of middle-class Hindu women took to the city's streets to promote swadeshi.

items.title: A pinch of salt for 1,600 rupees
items.summary: A pinch of salt that Gandhi made himself reportedly sold for 1,600 rupees.
